### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2025](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2025/summary/)

> “for having explained innovation-driven economic growth”

[Joel Mokyr](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2025/mokyr/facts/)

> “for having identified the prerequisites for sustained growth through technological progress”

[Philippe Aghion](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2025/aghion/facts/) and [Peter Howitt](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2025/howitt/facts/)

> “for the theory of sustained growth through creative destruction”

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2024](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2024/summary/)

[Daron Acemoglu](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2024/acemoglu/facts/), [Simon Johnson](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2024/johnson/facts/) and [James A. Robinson](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2024/robinson/facts/)

> “for studies of how institutions are formed and affect prosperity”

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2023](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2023/summary/)

[Claudia Goldin](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2023/goldin/facts/)

> “for having advanced our understanding of women’s labour market outcomes”

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2022](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2022/summary/)

[Ben Bernanke](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2022/bernanke/facts/), [Douglas Diamond](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2022/diamond/facts/) and [Philip Dybvig](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2022/dybvig/facts/)

> “for research on banks and financial crises”

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2021](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2021/summary/)

[David Card](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2021/card/facts/)

118|The announcement of the 2008 [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") in Nobel Prize Press Conference. The laureate of the Prize was [Paul Krugman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Krugman "Paul Krugman").
119|
120|The **Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences**, officially the **Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of [Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel")**[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): *Sveriges riksbanks pris i ekonomisk vetenskap till Alfred Nobels minne*), commonly referred to as the **Nobel Prize in Economics**, is an award in the field of [Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Sciences "Economic Sciences") administered by the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation").[[4]](#cite_note-NobelPrizeSelectionProcess-4)
121|
122|The first Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded in 1969 to [Ragnar Frisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragnar_Frisch "Ragnar Frisch") and [Jan Tinbergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Tinbergen "Jan Tinbergen").[[5]](#cite_note-Winners1969-5) Each recipient receives a [medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal "Medal"), a [diploma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diploma "Diploma") and a monetary award that has varied throughout the years.[[6]](#cite_note-NobelPrizeDescription-6) In 1969, Frisch and Tinbergen were given a combined 375,000 [SEK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"), which is equivalent to 2,871,041 SEK in December 2007. The award is presented in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm") at an annual ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death.[[7]](#cite_note-7)
123|
124|As of the awarding of the 2023 prize, 55 Prizes in Economic Sciences have been given to 93 individuals.[[8]](#cite_note-NobelLaureatesList-8) As of October 2023, the department of economics with the most affiliated [laureates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureate "Laureate") in economic sciences is the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago"),[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) with 16 affiliated laureates. As of 2023, the institutions with the most [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") (or equivalent) graduates who went on to receive the prize are Harvard University and MIT (13 each), followed by the University of Chicago (10). As of 2024, the institutions with the most affiliated faculty at the time of the award are the University of Chicago (15), followed by MIT (10), then by Princeton University and Harvard University (8 each).

118|The announcement of the 2008 [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") in Nobel Prize Press Conference. The laureate of the Prize was [Paul Krugman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Krugman "Paul Krugman").
119|
120|The **Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences**, officially the **Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of [Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel")**[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): *Sveriges riksbanks pris i ekonomisk vetenskap till Alfred Nobels minne*), commonly referred to as the **Nobel Prize in Economics**, is an award in the field of [Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Sciences "Economic Sciences") administered by the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation").[[4]](#cite_note-NobelPrizeSelectionProcess-4)
121|
122|The first Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded in 1969 to [Ragnar Frisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragnar_Frisch "Ragnar Frisch") and [Jan Tinbergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Tinbergen "Jan Tinbergen").[[5]](#cite_note-Winners1969-5) Each recipient receives a [medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal "Medal"), a [diploma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diploma "Diploma") and a monetary award that has varied throughout the years.[[6]](#cite_note-NobelPrizeDescription-6) In 1969, Frisch and Tinbergen were given a combined 375,000 [SEK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"), which is equivalent to 2,871,041 SEK in December 2007. The award is presented in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm") at an annual ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death.[[7]](#cite_note-7)
123|
124|As of the awarding of the 2023 prize, 55 Prizes in Economic Sciences have been given to 93 individuals.[[8]](#cite_note-NobelLaureatesList-8) As of October 2023, the department of economics with the most affiliated [laureates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureate "Laureate") in economic sciences is the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago"),[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) with 16 affiliated laureates. As of 2023, the institutions with the most [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") (or equivalent) graduates who went on to receive the prize are Harvard University and MIT (13 each), followed by the University of Chicago (10). As of 2024, the institutions with the most affiliated faculty at the time of the award are the University of Chicago (15), followed by MIT (10), then by Princeton University and Harvard University (8 each).

Ragnar Frisch  
 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 1969

Born: 3 March 1895, Oslo, Norway

Died: 31 January 1973, Oslo, Norway

Affiliation at the time of the award: University of Oslo, Oslo, Norway

Prize motivation: “for having developed and applied dynamic models for the analysis of economic processes”

Prize share: 1/2

### Life

Ragnar Frisch was born in Oslo, the son of a goldsmith, and he trained as a smith apprentice. His mother thought he should attend the university, and they chose economics as a subject because it seemed the shortest and easiest. After graduating in 1919, he studied economics and mathematics abroad for several years. He received his doctor’s degree in mathematical statistics in Oslo in 1926 and later became a professor. He married twice and had one daughter. Frisch’s hobby was beekeeping, something he described as an obsession.

### Work

Ragnar Frisch, along with Jan Tinbergen, pioneered development of mathematical formulations of economics. He coined the term econometrics for studies in which he used statistical methods to describe economic systems. He is best known for his contributions to dynamic economic modeling, and in 1933 he presented the first mathematical economic model that could describe fluctuations in the business cycle. His later work concerned models for economic planning.

Jan Tinbergen was born in The Hague and became interested in mathematics and natural science at an early age. Like Ragnar Frisch before him, Jan Tinbergen was a pioneer in changing economics from a science formulated in words to one based on mathematics. Tinbergen used his knowledge of statistics to test models in order to choose those that were most suitable.

Robert A. Mundell

Born: 24 October 1932, Kingston, ON, Canada

### Life

Robert Mundell was born in Kingston, Ontario, Canada. After studying at various universities around North America, he attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he received his Ph.D. in economics in 1956. In 1974 he joined Columbia University in New York, where he became University Professor in 2001. Mundell served as an advisor to several governments, including the US during Ronald Reagan’s presidency, and worked for international organisations such as the World Bank.

### Work

Exchange rates among different currencies are an important factor in business and the economy. In the beginning of the 1960s, Robert Mundell analyzed the effects of political actions on this area, including the consequences if exchange rates remain fixed or are allowed to be governed by the market. Mundell maintained that it could be advantageous for several countries to introduce a common currency, provided that the labor force has a great deal of mobility. Mundell’s theories had relevance for the introduction of the euro as the European Union’s currency.

This point was illustrated through his study of the insurance market, where the screening performed by insurance companies divides customers into risk classes.

# Daniel Kahneman

## Facts

![Image 1: Daniel Kahneman](blob:http://localhost/aef335eb562a1da6957ce25a574b4aa1)

Photo from the Nobel Foundation archive.

Daniel Kahneman

 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2002

Born: 5 March 1934, Tel Aviv, British Mandate of Palestine (now Israel)

Died: 27 March 2024

Affiliation at the time of the award: Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA

Prize motivation: “for having integrated insights from psychological research into economic science, especially concerning human judgment and decision-making under uncertainty”

Prize share: 1/2

### Life

Daniel Kahneman was born in Tel Aviv, Israel, while his mother was visiting her extended family. The family’s regular domicile was in Paris, France. After his father’s death in 1944, he moved with his mother and sister to Palestine. He studied psychology at Hebrew University and the University of California, earning his Ph.D. in 1961. Kahneman has been married twice and has two children.

### Work

Daniel Kahneman began his prize-awarded research in the late 1960s. In order to increase understanding of how people make economic decisions, he drew on cognitive psychology in relation to the mental process used in forming judgements and making choices. His research on decision-making under uncertainty resulted in the formulation of a new branch of economics, prospect theory.

Clive W.J. Granger  
 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2003

Born: 4 September 1934, Swansea, United Kingdom

Died: 27 May 2009, San Diego, CA, USA

Affiliation at the time of the award: University of California, San Diego, CA, USA

Prize motivation: “for methods of analyzing economic time series with common trends (cointegration)”

Prize share: 1/2

### Life

Clive Granger was born in Swansea, U.K. At the age of six, while his father was serving in WWII, the family moved to Cambridge. He applied to Nottingham University to study mathematics and economics. He received his Ph.D. in 1956. In 1974 he became a professor at the University of California, USA. Granger wrote several books, covering such subjects as time series analysis and forecasting, statistical theory and applied statistics.

### Work

Most macroeconomic time series follow a stochastic trend, so that a temporary disturbance in, say, GDP has a long-lasting effect. These time series are called nonstationary. Clive Granger demonstrated that the statistical method used for stationary time series could yield wholly misleading results when applied to analysis of nonstationary data. He developed methods that can be used to analyze the relations between for example wealth and consumption and exchange rates and price levels.

# [Nobel Prize](https://www.nobelprize.org)



# Edmund S. Phelps

## Facts

Photo: R. Talaie

Edmund S. Phelps  
 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2006

Born: 26 July 1933, Evanston, IL, USA

Died: 15 May 2026

Affiliation at the time of the award: Columbia University, New York, NY, USA

Prize motivation: “for his analysis of intertemporal tradeoffs in macroeconomic policy”

Prize share: 1/1

### Life

Edmund Phelps spent his school years in Hastings-on-Hudson, New York. He was an avid trumpet player, and credits the creative environment where he grew up as a major influence in his life. He went on to study at Yale where he received his Ph.D. in 1959. Phelps has taught and conducted research at several institutions in the U.S. In 1974 he married Viviana Montdor.

### Work

Edmund Phelps was awarded the Prize in Economic Sciences for his analysis of intertemporal trade-offs in macroeconomic policy, especially with regard to inflation, wages, and unemployment. In the late 1960s Phelps began his prize-awarded work, which challenged the assumption that high levels of unemployment corresponded with low levels of inflation and vice versa.

# [Nobel Prize](https://www.nobelprize.org)



# Leonid Hurwicz

## Facts

© University of Minnesota Photo: E. Ayoubzadeh

Leonid Hurwicz  
 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2007

Born: 21 August 1917, Moscow, Russia

Died: 24 June 2008, Minneapolis, MN, USA

Affiliation at the time of the award: University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, USA

Prize motivation: “for having laid the foundations of mechanism design theory”

Prize share: 1/3

### Life

Leonid Hurwicz was born in Moscow. In 1919, he and his family relocated to Warzaw, his father’s hometown. Hurwicz graduated from Warsaw University in 1938 with a degree in law. Due to Hitler’s rise to power, Hurwicz moved around Europe before leaving for Chicago in 1940. In the 1960s he started working on the mechanism design theory, the groundbreaking work that earned him the Prize in Economic Sciences.

### Work

Leonid Hurwicz started working on mechanism design theory in the 1960s. The theory allows us to distinguish situations in which markets work well from those in which they do not. It has helped economists identify efficient trading mechanisms, regulation schemes and voting procedures.

# Roger B. Myerson

## Facts

© The Nobel Foundation Photo: U. Montan

Roger B. Myerson  
 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2007

Born: 29 March 1951, Boston, MA, USA

Affiliation at the time of the award: University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA

Prize motivation: “for having laid the foundations of mechanism design theory”

Prize share: 1/3

### Life

Roger Myerson grew up in Boston, U.S.A. He attended Harvard University, where he completed his Ph.D. in applied mathematics in 1976. It was during these studies Myerson became interested in game theory, a small field in the 1970s. Myerson took a position at Northwestern University, Illinois, where he conducted most of his Prize-awarded research. He is married with two children.

### Work

In 1972, while studying at Harvard, Myerson took a course on game theory, which then became his main research subject. He conducted much of his Prize-awarded research at Northwestern University, Illinois, where he was a professor from 1976-2001. He was awarded the Prize in Economic Sciences in recognition of his contributions to mechanism design theory, which analyzes rules for coordinating economic agents efficiently when they have different information and difficulty trusting each other.

### Work

International trade has long been a central issue in economic science. Economies of scale and reduced transport costs also explain why an increasing proportion of people live and work in cities.

# All prizes in economic sciences

The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel has been awarded 57 times to 99 laureates between 1969 and 2025. Click on the links to get more information.

* * *

## Find all prizes in | [physics](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-nobel-prizes-in-physics/) | [chemistry](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-nobel-prizes-in-chemistry/) | [physiology or medicine](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-nobel-laureates-in-physiology-or-medicine/) | [literature](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-nobel-prizes-in-literature/) | [peace](http://nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-nobel-peace-prizes/) | [economic sciences](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-prizes-in-economic-sciences/) | [all categories](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-nobel-prizes/)

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2025](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2025/summary/)

> “for having explained innovation-driven economic growth”

[Joel Mokyr](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2025/mokyr/facts/)

> “for having identified the prerequisites for sustained growth through technological progress”

[Philippe Aghion](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2025/aghion/facts/) and [Peter Howitt](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2025/howitt/facts/)

> “for the theory of sustained growth through creative destruction”

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2024](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2024/summary/)

[Daron Acemoglu](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2024/acemoglu/facts/), [Simon Johnson](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2024/johnson/facts/) and [James A. Robinson](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2024/robinson/facts/)

> “for studies of how institutions are formed and affect prosperity”

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2023](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2023/summary/)

[Claudia Goldin](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2023/goldin/facts/)

> “for having advanced our understanding of women’s labour market outcomes”

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2022](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2022/summary/)

[Ben Bernanke](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2022/bernanke/facts/), [Douglas Diamond](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2022/diamond/facts/) and [Philip Dybvig](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2022/dybvig/facts/)

> “for research on banks and financial crises”

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2021](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2021/summary/)

[David Card](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2021/card/facts/)

> “for his empirical contributions to labour economics”

[Joshua D. Angrist](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2021/angrist/facts/) and [Guido W. Imbens](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2021/imbens/facts/)

> “for their methodological contributions to the analysis of causal relationships”

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2020](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2020/summary/)

[Paul R. Milgrom](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2020/milgrom/facts/) and [Robert B. Wilson](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2020/wilson/facts/)

> “for improvements to auction theory and inventions of new auction formats”

118|The announcement of the 2008 [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") in Nobel Prize Press Conference. The laureate of the Prize was [Paul Krugman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Krugman "Paul Krugman").
119|
120|The **Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences**, officially the **Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of [Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel")**[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): *Sveriges riksbanks pris i ekonomisk vetenskap till Alfred Nobels minne*), commonly referred to as the **Nobel Prize in Economics**, is an award in the field of [Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Sciences "Economic Sciences") administered by the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation").[[4]](#cite_note-NobelPrizeSelectionProcess-4)
121|
122|The first Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded in 1969 to [Ragnar Frisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragnar_Frisch "Ragnar Frisch") and [Jan Tinbergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Tinbergen "Jan Tinbergen").[[5]](#cite_note-Winners1969-5) Each recipient receives a [medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal "Medal"), a [diploma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diploma "Diploma") and a monetary award that has varied throughout the years.[[6]](#cite_note-NobelPrizeDescription-6) In 1969, Frisch and Tinbergen were given a combined 375,000 [SEK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"), which is equivalent to 2,871,041 SEK in December 2007. The award is presented in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm") at an annual ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death.[[7]](#cite_note-7)
123|
124|As of the awarding of the 2023 prize, 55 Prizes in Economic Sciences have been given to 93 individuals.[[8]](#cite_note-NobelLaureatesList-8) As of October 2023, the department of economics with the most affiliated [laureates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureate "Laureate") in economic sciences is the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago"),[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) with 16 affiliated laureates. As of 2023, the institutions with the most [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") (or equivalent) graduates who went on to receive the prize are Harvard University and MIT (13 each), followed by the University of Chicago (10). As of 2024, the institutions with the most affiliated faculty at the time of the award are the University of Chicago (15), followed by MIT (10), then by Princeton University and Harvard University (8 each).

197|The [Nobel Prizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize") ([Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"): _Nobelpriset_, [Norwegian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_language "Norwegian language"): _Nobelprisen_) are awarded annually by the [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences"), the [Swedish Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Academy "Swedish Academy"), the [Karolinska Institutet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karolinska_Institute "Karolinska Institute"), and the [Norwegian Nobel Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Nobel_Committee "Norwegian Nobel Committee") to individuals and organizations who make outstanding contributions in the fields of [chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Chemistry "Nobel Prize in Chemistry"), [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics"), [literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "Nobel Prize in Literature"), [peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize"), and [physiology or medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine "Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-1) They were established by the 1895 will of [Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel"), which dictates that the awards should be administered by the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation"). An additional prize in memory of Alfred Nobel was established in 1968 by [Sveriges Riksbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sveriges_Riksbank "Sveriges Riksbank") (Sweden's [central bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_bank "Central bank")) for outstanding contributions to the field of [economics](https://en.wikipedia.or... [truncated]

199|## Prize
200|
201|Different organisations are responsible for awarding the individual prizes; the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awards the Prizes in Physics, Chemistry, and Economics; the Swedish Academy awards the Prize in Literature; the Karolinska Institute awards the Prize in Physiology or Medicine; and the Norwegian Nobel Committee awards the Prize in Peace.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-3) Each recipient receives a medal, a diploma and a monetary award that has varied throughout the years.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-NobelPrizeDescription-2) In 1901, the recipients of the first Nobel Prizes were given 150,782 [SEK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"), equivalent to 10.8 million SEK in 2023. In 2017, the laureates were awarded a prize amount of 9 million SEK.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-4) The awards are presented in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm") in an annual ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-5)
202|
203|In years in which the Nobel Prize is not awarded due to external events or a lack of nominations, the prize money is returned to the funds delegated to the relevant prize.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-Winners1942-6) The Nobel Prize was not awarded between 1940 and 1942 due to the outbreak of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-PeacePrizeArticle-7)

205|## Laureates
206|
207|Between 1901 and 2017, the [Nobel Prizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prizes "Nobel Prizes") and the [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") were awarded 585 times to 923 people and organizations. With some receiving the Nobel Prize more than once, this makes a total of 892 individuals (including 844 men, 48 women) and 24 organizations.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-8) Six Nobel laureates were not permitted by their governments to accept the Nobel Prize. [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") forbade four Germans, [Richard Kuhn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Kuhn "Richard Kuhn") (Chemistry, 1938), [Adolf Butenandt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Butenandt "Adolf Butenandt") (Chemistry, 1939), [Gerhard Domagk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerhard_Domagk "Gerhard Domagk") (Physiology or Medicine, 1939) and [Carl von Ossietzky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_von_Ossietzky "Carl von Ossietzky") (Peace, 1936) from accepting their Nobel Prizes. The [Chinese government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China") forbade [Liu Xiaobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Xiaobo "Liu Xiaobo") from accepting his Nobel Prize (Peace, 2010)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-9) and the government of the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") pressured [Boris Pasternak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Pasternak "Boris Pasternak") (Literature, 1958) to decline his award. [Liu Xiaobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Xiaobo "Liu Xiaobo"), [Carl von Ossietzky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_von_Ossietzky "Carl von Ossietzky") and [Aung San Suu Kyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aung_San_Suu_Kyi "Aung San Suu Kyi") were all awarded their Nobel Prize while in prison... [truncated]
208|
209|Seven laureates have received more than one prize; of the seven, the [International Committee of the Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Committee_of_the_Red_Cross "International Committee of the Red Cross") has received the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") three times, more than any other.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-NobelFacts-11)[UNHCR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNHCR "UNHCR") (United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees) has been awarded the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") twice. Also the [Nobel Prize in Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics") was awarded to [John Bardeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bardeen "John Bardeen") twice, as was the [Nobel Prize in Chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Chemistry "Nobel Prize in Chemistry") to [Frederick Sanger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Sanger "Frederick Sanger") and [Karl Barry Sharpless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Barry_Sharpless "Karl Barry Sharpless"). Two laureates have been awarded twice but not in the same field: [Marie Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie "Marie Curie") (Physics and Chemistry) and [Linus Pauling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linus_Pauling "Linus Pauling") (Chemistry and Peace). Among the 892 Nobel laureates, 48 have been women; the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize was [Marie Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Curie "Marie Curie"), who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-WomenLaureates-12) She was also the first person (male or female) to be awarded two Nobel Prizes, the second award being the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, given in 1911.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#cite_note-NobelFacts-11)

# Nobel Prize laureates and research affiliations

![Image 1: Big building surrounded by autumn leaves](https://www.nobelprize.org/images//158921-landscape-x-large.jpg)

Matthews Hall, Harvard University.Photo: Daderot, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

This list shows the universities, research institutions or companies Nobel Prize laureates were affiliated with at the time of the Nobel Prize announcement.

## A.F. Ioffe Physico-Technical Institute, St. Petersburg, Russia (1)

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2000](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2000/summary/)

> “for basic work on information and communication technology”

[Zhores Alferov](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2000/alferov/facts/) and [Herbert Kroemer](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2000/kroemer/facts/)

> “for developing semiconductor heterostructures used in high-speed- and opto-electronics”

[Jack Kilby](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2000/kilby/facts/)

> “for his part in the invention of the integrated circuit”

## Aarhus University, Aarhus, Denmark (2)

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2010](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2010/summary/)

[Peter A. Diamond](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2010/diamond/facts/), [Dale T. Mortensen](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2010/mortensen/facts/) and [Christopher A. Pissarides](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2010/pissarides/facts/)

> “for their analysis of markets with search frictions”

### [Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1997](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1997/summary/)

[Paul D. Boyer](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1997/boyer/facts/) and [John E. Walker](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1997/walker/facts/)

> “for their elucidation of the enzymatic mechanism underlying the synthesis of adenosine triphosphate (ATP)”

[Jens C. Skou](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1997/skou/facts/)

> “for the first discovery of an ion-transporting enzyme, Na+, K+ -ATPase”

## Academy of Sciences, Moscow, USSR (now Russia) (3)

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 1962](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1962/summary/)

[Lev Landau](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1962/landau/facts/)

> “for his pioneering theories for condensed matter, especially liquid helium”

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 1975](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/1975/summary/)

[Leonid Vitaliyevich Kantorovich](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/1975/kantorovich/facts/) and [Tjalling C. Koopmans](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/1975/koopmans/facts/)

> “for their contributions to the theory of optimum allocation of resources”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 1978](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1978/summary/)

[Pyotr Kapitsa](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1978/kapitsa/facts/)

> “for his basic inventions and discoveries in the area of low-temperature physics”

[Arno Penzias](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1978/penzias/facts/) and [Robert Woodrow Wilson](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1978/wilson/facts/)

> “for their discovery of cosmic microwave background radiation”

## All Souls College, Oxford, United Kingdom (1)

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 1972](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/1972/summary/)

[John R. Hicks](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/1972/hicks/facts/) and [Kenneth J. Arrow](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/1972/arrow/facts/)

> “for their pioneering contributions to general economic equilibrium theory and welfare theory”

## Amsterdam University, Amsterdam, the Netherlands (2)

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 1910](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1910/summary/)

[Johannes Diderik van der Waals](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1910/waals/facts/)

> “for his work on the equation of state for gases and liquids”

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 1902](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1902/summary/)

[Hendrik A. Lorentz](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1902/lorentz/facts/) and [Pieter Zeeman](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1902/zeeman/facts/)

> “in recognition of the extraordinary service they rendered by their researches into the influence of magnetism upon radiation phenomena”

## Argonne National Laboratory, Argonne, IL, USA (1)

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2003](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2003/summary/)

[Alexei Abrikosov](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2003/abrikosov/facts/), [Vitaly L. Ginzburg](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2003/ginzburg/facts/) and [Anthony J. Leggett](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2003/leggett/facts/)

> “for pioneering contributions to the theory of superconductors and superfluids”

## Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, USA (2)

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2009](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2009/summary/)

[Elinor Ostrom](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2009/ostrom/facts/)

> “for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons”

[Oliver E. Williamson](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2009/williamson/facts/)

> “for his analysis of economic governance, especially the boundaries of the firm”

### [Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2004](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2004/summary/)

[Finn E. Kydland](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2004/kydland/facts/) and [Edward C. Prescott](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2004/prescott/facts/)

> “for their contributions to dynamic macroeconomics: the time consistency of economic policy and the driving forces behind business cycles”

## Asahi Kasei Corporation, Tokyo, Japan (1)

### [Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2019](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2019/summary/)

[John B. Goodenough](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2019/goodenough/facts/), [M. Stanley Whittingham](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2019/whittingham/facts/) and [Akira Yoshino](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2019/yoshino/facts/)

> “for the development of lithium-ion batteries”

## Associated Universities Inc., Washington, D.C., USA (1)

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2002](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2002/summary/)

[Raymond Davis Jr.](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2002/davis/facts/) and [Masatoshi Koshiba](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2002/koshiba/facts/)

> “for pioneering contributions to astrophysics, in particular for the detection of cosmic neutrinos”

[Riccardo Giacconi](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2002/giacconi/facts/)

> “for pioneering contributions to astrophysics, which have led to the discovery of cosmic X-ray sources”

## Atomic Energy Research Establishment, Harwell, Berkshire, United Kingdom (1)

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 1951](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1951/summary/)

[John Cockcroft](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1951/cockcroft/facts/) and [Ernest T.S. Walton](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1951/walton/facts/)

> “for their pioneer work on the transmutation of atomic nuclei by artificially accelerated atomic particles”

## Australian National University, Canberra, Australia (1)

### [Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1963](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1963/summary/)

[Sir John Eccles](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1963/eccles/facts/), [Alan Hodgkin](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1963/hodgkin/facts/) and [Andrew Huxley](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1963/huxley/facts/)

> “for their discoveries concerning the ionic mechanisms involved in excitation and inhibition in the peripheral and central portions of the nerve cell membrane”

## Australian National University, Weston Creek, Australia (1)

### [Nobel Prize in Physics 2011](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2011/summary/)

[Saul Perlmutter](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2011/perlmutter/facts/), [Brian P. Schmidt](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2011/schmidt/facts/) and [Adam G. Riess](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2011/riess/facts/)

> “for the discovery of the accelerating expansion of the Universe through observations of distant supernovae”

## Basel Institute for Immunology, Basel, Switzerland (2)

### [Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1984](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1984/summary/)

[Niels K. Jerne](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1984/jerne/facts/), [Georges J.F. Köhler](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1984/kohler/facts/) and [César Milstein](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1984/milstein/facts/)

> “for theories concerning the specificity in development and control of the immune system and the discovery of the principle for production of monoclonal antibodies”

### [Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1984](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1984/summary/)

[Niels K. Jerne](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1984/jerne/facts/), [Georges J.F. Köhler](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1984/kohler/facts/) and [César Milstein](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1984/milstein/facts/)

> “for theories concerning the specificity in development and control of the immune system and the discovery of the principle for production of monoclonal antibodies”

### [Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1973](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1973/summary/)

[Karl von Frisch](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1973/frisch/facts/), [Konrad Lorenz](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1973/lorenz/facts/) and [Nikolaas Tinbergen](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1973/tinbergen/facts/)
